blocks.x: I'll make a note on here that we're interviewing Mr. Louis Kepard at his home at 1017 North Villary, is that right? That's right. And the date is January the 19th, 1961. And you might give your full name if you have a middle name.
Louis Kepard.
Just Louis Kepard.
Yes, sir.
You pronounce that Kepard sort of a French accent.
K-E-P-A-R-D Kepard. It's the same name as Freddie Kepard. You see? Yes. Now, that's my oldest brother I had. I had four altogether, but the rest of the other two died while I was young.
You might give your birth date if you don't mind.
Well, born February the 2nd, 1889. And may I ask you a question, Mr. Certainly. Well, I want to find out, do you want to find out about bands and different things right now?

Yes. Anything, it doesn't have to be in any special order, but just anything that you happen to think of. We might ask a little bit more about your family. Did your father or mother play any instruments? No, they're nothing whatever.
They just brought us up. The first thing we started on, he started on a violin. I believe I gave it to you, Mr. Yes. We have the mandolin.
The mandolin.

The mandolin. And he had a violin, but of course by me he left him to lay up and lay up and it just went to the jump power. Which did he start on, the violin or the mandolin? The violin first and then after the mandolin. Then he started with the card game. Then he played harmonica. When he was playing harmonica, then the last thing he picked up was the violin and I had a guitar with my mother and father. I was like a guitar, you know, I can't hear me. It wasn't a guitar exactly, but it was made out of old boxwood. And well I must have been about, say about seven, eight years old. And she used to bring us around different corners to our friends. And Freddie used to have his violin, I had an old guitar, just hit and didn't know what I was doing or whatever. I was just thumping on it and didn't know if it was B-flap to G or F or C or nothing. I just hit on it. Well of course the people had liked us because we were so young to be going around and we used to take and talk. How old were you then? Well I must have been about nine years old and he must have been about eight because I'm older than Freddie. So you're going to say about a year younger than you? Not quite a year, but Freddie ought to be about 71 years old now. How old is that you're 72? And I'm 72. Now February the 2nd I'll be 73. February coming. Well I'll be 73 years old. Well about a month after that I'll be about 72. And of course I have my sister when she's old. She's like that much. Your wife mentioned that your sister's living here now. Yeah that's what I got back then. You said she'd be 79 in February? She'd be 79 in February. She'd be 79 in February. February the 15th. February the 15th she'd be 79. Does she remember much about the family? I wonder if she'd be able to give us an interview. Do you think she would mind it? Well I'll tell you.
I would like to do it. But of course now as the doctor gives her up and says look to you for her. I'll bring her home. She has a stroke. She's had a stroke. And uh well she had to bring her home.

She can't hardly explain her words. See and then a stroke makes her walk on her bed. And she'd have to drag her foot. So I had to bring her home from where she was living on St. Fella Street. 1827 St. Fella. So I brought her home. And I brought her home. And she'd be able to be able to give us an interview. Do you think she would mind it? Well I'll tell you. I would like to do it. But of course now as the doctor gives her up and say look to you for her. I'd bring her home. She had a stroke. She had a stroke. And uh well she had to bring her home. Well she had to bring her home. Because she had a stroke, make her walk on her bed. And she'd have to drag her foot. So I had to bring her home from where she was living on St. Fella Street. 1827 St. Fella. So I brought her home. And I had to move all the things over here. As we had sufficient enough place to put it. Well of course my wife, she was the one that suggested to bring her home. Because people don't like to have trouble with you when you get so old, you get sicker. Somebody got to take care of you. So I just said, well, me and my wife got together and I brought her home. So that's where, well, we have plenty of trouble with her now. Don't say that.

We got plenty of trouble with her. I'm wondering, speaking of the family, just where were you born? You remember, of course, you don't remember. I mean, but where was the house and which street were you and Freddie when you were children? Well, when we were children, we were staying on Custom House Street.

It's Ivorville now, but it was Custom House during that time. And we was kids. We was young kids. That's where we was born at. You remember the number? It was 2007, Custom House Street. Near Jalapen. Near Preff. It was on the uptown side of the banking. And, of course, we were small. That's where we were born at. Now, my sister, she was born right there herself. Of course, there's three of us. But my other brothers, well, of course, they was young. I don't know exactly. But that was Custom House Street at that time. But it's out of Hill Street now. Now, is there any other thing that I can...
You say none of your family, your mother and father, didn't play anything at all? None, whatever. They just played us. Did they play?

Pardon me? Did any of your parents sing? Well, none of them sing. Of course, see, Freddie was just like a jive, just like myself, I guess. And he never was a song to me. He was just only an intro player. That's all. Like myself. Of course, he was a good comedian. You know, full of bull stuff.
Yeah.
He put me in a mind. This fellow was up there. Now, I'm really Armstrong. But Lewis got the best go now, you know.
Yeah, that's right.

But he was very... He wasn't born, I believe, when he was coming out. No. No. Lewis used to work for W.G. Carl Coop. Now, I remember when he was a little small kid, living on Saratoga in Potters. Well, of course, them days, we didn't know nothing about Lewis, but Lewis started at home. They tell me.
How about your other brothers and sisters? Did they ever play anything?
No, they was young and they died young.
Just you and Freddie?

Just me and Freddie. Uh-huh. Whatever. Your older sister didn't play anything? My older sister, she never played nothing. She used to be working for Dr. Bartley, a dentist up down there. Well, that's all she ever done. Worked in the dentist place and filled teeth and all that, you know. My father, he was a cook at Fred Boytrand on Dauphin and Canal. That's been, oh, years back when I was a little kid. What was that? Restaurant there? That was a restaurant and a bar. Well, of course, I'll tell you. When I was a kid, my dad was there and I don't want to exaggerate, but that was the time I was a small kid. I must have been about 11 years old at that time. They had to call, it was like a riot down here one time. And I believe they called, I'm more sure, I know it positively, this fellow is Robert Charles. Oh, yes. And that's been some time back. I think that was about 1900. Oh, a little longer than that. Robert Charles. Well, they had almost a riot down here.
You would have been about 11 years old.

Well, I must have been about 11 years old at that time or 10, between 10 and 11. Well, of course, my daddy used to be the head cook at Fred Boytrand on Dauphin and Canal. The rest of the way KB's is now. Oh, yes. Right there where KB's is now. Was that for white or color? That was for white. For white. But my daddy was the head cook. Yeah. Had all that big old pots and different things and chef and everything and chef cook, you know. Yeah. Well, of course, you see my daddy, eh?
Uh, the photographs you made? Yeah. Let me think. I don't remember now. Well, when you have a spare time. When you have a spare time. It must have changed. You've shown it to me before.

When you have a spare time, I'll let you see his photograph because I got it from my sister. I got it over here. She had it and brought it here. I got it over here. Well, it's a T4 from here. I done framed it. Oh, yeah. And I framed it with Freddie and myself and my Freddie, my daddy, and myself up in that frame up there. When you get ready, you can, oh, yeah. You can take and just take and look at it as long as you wish to look at it. That's what the Magnolia... That's the Magnolia band with Jew Oliver.
Yeah.
That's Jew Oliver in that time when I was the manager of the band.

Now, is there any other subject I would like to... I was wondering anything else about your neighborhood when you were a kid. Do you remember any parades up there or any other dance halls or anything around the neighborhood when you were very small?

Well, I was very small. What kind of music you heard when you were a little kid? Well, when I was small, I used to hear them. They had two white bands right across from me. And that was on Custom House Street between Fred and Johnson. And I was shining shoes at the proper time in the district. And Freddie was also shining shoes. That was pretty close to the district where you lived then, wasn't it? Well, then I moved from Iverville, from Custom House Street to Viro. And that was 427, not Viro Street. That was between St. Louis and Conti. But near St. Louis. About how old were you? I must have been about, say, about 12 years old then.

Well, I was going to ask some more if you remember anything else about the riot. You started to say something about that. Was your father mixed up in it anyway? Well, no, whatever. Or do you remember it?

No, my father wasn't mixed up in it. Because my father, he could pass around the streets. And they wouldn't worry him. Because my father was a Creole. And you know, in Creole, well, my father was kind of bright.
Yes.
And they couldn't tell him from who's who.
Yeah.
See? Of course, it's like this François Michaud down there when I used to play. You couldn't tell who's who. I guess right now, all of them is all mixed up. You can't tell who's who now.
Yeah.

And my dad was just like, he was French, but he had this, like Italian, and you couldn't tell him from French, you couldn't tell him from Italian, but he's French. Yeah. His mother was French, I suppose. And, well, of course, it was all jubileed up. Yeah. Well, so when he went to street, it's all right. Just like anything else, well, they'll pass over him, like they pass over a lot of people in the streets now. You can't tell who's who these days in time. Yes. That's right. That's what I said. We ought to be careful who we contact with, because we don't know who's who these days in time. You can't put your finger in the fire for the other fellow, because you don't know exactly who he is. See? Because the whole thing is, when you know a person from birth, then you can tell who he is. So I said, well, my father was all right. But when I went to the place, I was in short pants, and my cousin, he used to work as a dishwasher under my daddy. They called him Cloppy. Of course, he was here yesterday to see my sister. Of course, he's very stout. He used to work for that drug assault in St. Philip and Claiborne. And they called him Edmund Glapion. But he was working there, but of course, he had to slip soon in the morning to get there, because he wasn't much more fat than I was. Of course, my mother left me go, but she didn't know the trouble that my father got home and had to keep it until night. Then I had to slip me in, because he was shooting down and making humbugs in the streets. Yeah, all over. All over the hotel. You see? Because, man, you know, they'd break him like, I guess, like that school going on now and everything else.

Yeah. The only word must have been worse at that time. It's his voice. Do you remember, if I remember rightly, Big Eye Louie, you know, Louie Nelson, the clarinet player, I think said his father was killed in that riot. Do you remember? Did he ever tell you anything about it? Well, I didn't know Louie's father, whatever. I didn't know him. I don't know what. I mean, did Louie ever tell you anything about it?

No. He never said nothing about it. The only thing I've been knowing Louie for a couple of years, and I see a barque and George Barque, and I knew it was all them barqueers. One of them used to play a lot of bands, you know, on the other side. Yeah. Of course, I understand he's right between lines on the other side. Yeah. And, of course, I played with him. I think he's dead now, too.
He's dead.
John's dead. John's dead. And Ashiel's dead. But, of course, Ashiel was a clarinet player. He was tough.
Did you ever work with him, too?

Oh, yeah, I worked with him. I did. Before you left him. I worked with him, and then after that, he crossed over. Yeah. Well, then they got some of the white boys. They liked the way he played, heard him, and they knew he was a clarinet player, and they just used him. Yeah. Then after that, they used him a couple of times, and he stuck.
Yeah.
Well, after he stuck, well, he forgot about the other fellow, what he used to be with.
Yeah.
Well, of course, I understand. I don't blame him. Of course, there was more money. There was more money in that than with us.
He wanted that. See? I couldn't blame him, I guess.

Then what happened to him is he went too far, I guess. And the wildestad, that he takes and went and started fooling around, fooling around. After he got so bright on clarinet, and so perfect on a clarinet, and making the baby cry, and all that, and the other fellows were having a good time. So he figured he'd have a good time. And after that, they found him out that they said, when we called for a white band, we want some white band. We don't want a colored band. So that would knock him out. So after you're knocking him out there, well, I see, well, he had to take and leave. Or they went to Chicago or somewhere.
I think you met Los Angeles finally. He died out there.

Exactly. But I know that's the trouble today, that they found it out. They was colored, and they know it all the time. But as long as he was in his place, he was solid. But the minute that he overcome his jurisdiction, then he takes and he fell down. Like the old words say, who fell down, stayed down. So he went down. And he had to get out of the band. Then he takes and go to California somewhere, as I don't exactly know. But I knew he hurt his own self in the band. So any other thing, Mr.
Do you remember George Barquet, the one that played with your brother? Can you tell us anything much about him? Do you remember George?

George Barquet. Yeah, I played with him. George was a good clarinet player, too. And he is a player of funerals. And he was a funer man. He didn't miss a lick. He was right there on the job. Well, I tell you, if I am mistaken, I believe he was a better musician. Not in the line of musician, but in the line of playing, I believe he was better than Alphonse Piku. In a funeral. Because he used to play some tough music, and he used to make that clarinet cry like a baby. He was solid. He was good. Of course, Piku is all right, but he's variation. But George used to put on this lead improvisation, you know? And that lead is the main thing, and put everything in its place. And I remember seeing students where George used to blow that clarinet with his head up in the air, and George taking head people around that crime.
That's what I've heard other people, too, and told me that, too.

And that song, I'll never forget that song, but I don't know exactly the words, but I sure would like to know the words of that. But I can always hum the words. And what's it like? If you don't mind, I'll hum the words.
Every time you enjoy it.
It goes like this. It's gosh, gosh, gosh. I
I
I I I I I
I I I I I I I I I

I George with that clarinet, he'd make them what they call shriveling that clarinet. And Mario Perez, he was playing with Mario Perez's brass band. And Mario used to be the leading and he used to be making nothing but just crying in that clarinet. Of course I understand.
But it was a slow funeral of dirt.

No, I remember four times. Yeah. Flow four. Now, Mario would make the lead. Of course they used Pico and all that, but now and that, but they didn't lead no more than him. And he used to have that clarinet going. Now another one he was good too, and he was clumsy, Lorenzo Teo. He was tough. His daddy was alright, but not like Lorenzo Teo. See but the whole thing is Lorenzo Teo, he was just like Bechet. Bechet is one of them. He was a good clarinet. Of course I understand. He went away and he played for the Queen, the King and everything else. He was a clarinet player. But he was a clarinet player. And he used to have rubber, just like Lorenzo Teo used to have rubber on the clarinet when he come to play on the job. He's clarinet full of rubber. But Bechet takes a while. My piece and play this by himself. Don't need the whole stick. Somebody else tell me that. See? Of course he used to take and be, he used to be in that market. He used to sleep on the meat stand. You know they had a market there right there on the Seminar and Flavorne before that grocery went there. That's a circle there. But it used to be a meat stand there. It was. I didn't know. How about that grocery? How was that in there? Well, there was a meat stand. They had butchers up in there. And then, of course, since this man bought it, well he put his gross up in there. Now they call it the circle. The, I mean the circle market. But that was nothing but a big butcher stand. So of course Bechet used to be up in there. And they used to have an alley back there. Well, that pig, they probably used to shine shoes back there. And Bechet used to sleep on the stand back there. Wouldn't even go home to sleep. Wouldn't go home. Of course, I don't know if he had a home. I don't know at that time he was young, you know. And of course the boys was mischievous. But they ain't bad like they is now. They'd go and rest theirself and go lay down somebody, around somebody. But now they don't rest until they get a hold of a pocketbook.
Unless they knock your brains loose.
If you got them, if you ain't got them, they'll knock your brains loose, you know. Can you tell us anything about the Block A family?
Did you ever know of George's parents or any of the family?

Well, George, when I noticed, I went to his house on Roman, between right, on Roman, between Beville and Abbeville. Of course, I can't say Custom House because he was in Chicago. But I met his wife. And he come home from Chicago and I met his wife over there. There was about the 200 block of Bright Cross from, I don't know if you heard talk about this man, Gross, on Beville and Prayer. No, I don't think I know. Well, that's the way, that's the way he's at, Gross, Paul Gross. Mm-hmm. The Bible and Roman, I want to say, but George Barquet, when he come home sick, his sister was sick, his wife and his sister was living on Roman between Abbeville and Beville. Well, that's where he died at. See? Did you, you saw him after he came back from Chicago? Yeah, I seen him. I seen him, but he was sick. He was sick then. And that's where he died around there. I went to his house and seen him. Then I, when he died, well, I went to see him at the wake.
Do you remember, did his father play some instrument or was he in the band?

Old Man Barquet. Yeah, he used to play clarinet, Old Man Barquet. Old Man Barquet. If I'm mistaken, of course I was very young. I believe if I'm mistaken, I believe that's the one who taught George how to play and his brother. Of course you couldn't tell now, Achille Barquet and George Barquet, well, that's the old man who used to play clarinet too. Now, of course they used to have a band by the name of Alexander, but I ain't talking about that young fella now. He's paralyzed. He's got a stroke, I believe. But I'm talking about the old man.
I've seen his picture. He's playing off the horn right there.

That's right. He's dead now. And of course he used to play clarinet. He was a good musician. He used to be a director. He's almost like Chalini. I guess you were talking about Chalini. Of course I'm talking about them old timers like this fella here. Well, that's old time too. John Parker. Yes, I know him. John Parker? Willie. Willie Popper. Live off St. Philip's straight there. Well, I know him. Well, of course I can't mention the young fellas these days in time because they're coming up like they come from underneath the ground on me. Yeah. Because I don't know him. Of course I'm out of the picture, that's what I say. Of course it's like a fella get 50, 60, I hate him no more because he doesn't got too old.
You're still working when you run to work. You're still working with the Gibson band anyway.

Well, you see, well I'm working with old men and young men too. Yeah. But of course I didn't know the young fellas coming up now these days in time. I happen to be with the Gibson brass band now playing tubo with them. And the whole thing is I didn't know them when I first went there. But of course after taking and started playing with them a little while, the young ones like them as well as the old ones. Yeah. Of course I understand they got good and bad in all ways, you know. Sometime when they make a bus, well you got to try to cover that bus up.
Yeah.

See, the young ones make it, not the old ones can't make it. Yeah. Well of course the old ones make buses, while the young ones make it. Well that ought to be that they ought to have more of a better education now than, and more of a mother wit than what the older times, because they never had. You see in them days in time, Mr. Russel, in them days in time, we had the guests. We had the, we never had the teachers that they got today. Now today is the day you can get a teacher every minute in the day. You got teachers to learn you. But we just had to pick it up from the man above. God of mine to get a gift.
Did you get any help at all from any other guitar players that helped you?

Well I tell you, I was, I wasn't stopped. But I was only told how to do it while all the music stand with them. Yeah. And I was taking, asking them what do you call that, before I started playing guitar. And, because I wasn't playing a guitar when I was with my brother. I was, when Freddie had a violin I was just only hitting on it. But I wanted to learn to see what I was doing. Yeah. I wanted to, just like a fellow reading the paper. If he don't read it, he didn't, just looking at it, he can't get nothing out of it. Yeah. Well I wanted to get the sweetest out to get there, because I hear so many other fellows making that good harmony. So I thought I was taking, ask those things that I don't know, I'm going to ask for it. They say you ask, and you, and you'll get received. See, if you knock into the door, well you're bound, the door's bound to open to you. Well I used to take and go around, bands, and I met up this fellow, Willie Santiago.
Oh yes. I never knew him, I've heard of him.

Well he used to play with my brother. Well, he was a good guitar player, manly player, banjo player. He was a string hand, for instance, man. Well, he turned around and I see him and I say, Willie, I says, I says, how about, what is that you're making this now? So, I just have to buy him a little drink or something like that, you know, and I know he used to like his beer and his wine and all that. Well, I, you know, I was working, I had to work, because I never had no music on me, I never had nothing to learn, I never, I wasn't starting to play music. But I wanted to get off that job, where I was working at. See, I wanted to quit working, so I could make an easy money like them. Well, after that he showed me the stretches, tell me what it is, just like he said, well this is C natural, this is E flat. And I said, well Willie, well how about that? He said, well this is E flat. I said, well how about that? He said, well this is D natural. I said, well, alright, I said, don't show me all at one time, just show me one at a time, so I can go home and practice that on that old guitar I got home. Well, happened that I continued, so I never seen his band, I seen another one, Robichaud's band. Well, I, a mixer, I'll just go around, that's to make you see I talk so much now. Well, I got around Robichaud and said, how you all doing gentlemen? And I got in with all of them and I met Jonathan Seah. And I said, hello, he said, hello there boy, hello there partner. Well, I don't care what he said, I just got close to him and he couldn't make a move and I'll follow him. So I said, I said, Mr. Bud, what is that you making? Well, he said, well that's the way he talks, well I tell you, problem. I'll tell you. I said, I'm pretty careful. He says, oh yeah, well anyhow, this here is G, natural. I said, well, what is that other thing? He said, that's B flat. I said, oh yeah, I said, uh-huh. So I says, well, the only thing I could do, I done got so many, and every time I turn around, I goes and try to find out what's what all the time. I never had no time for the street. I had time just to go and find out, to learn something so I could quit working. Well, I just continued, continued, continued. So what I done, I went to Manuel Perez, and got in with him, and I asked him to learn me how to play corner, because me and my brother couldn't get along. Freddy and myself couldn't get along. We wasn't much, you know how brothers is, some of them. Well, one want to have his way, and the other fella tell him something, he gets mad, he want to let him know that he's the boss. Well, I just left Freddy Cole, so I just went to Manuel Perez and started learning. Well, Manuel Perez charged me, it was six bits of lesson that time. Well, I take him two lessons a week. Well, I says, well, Manuel, I says, what is this thing? So he showed me, gave me a line of music, made me get an auto language, and I said, well, all right, Manuel. I said, now, Manuel, I says, what must I say? He said, you see, that's where you got it, it's on the end of the line, it's one flat. He said, that's what they call F. He said, two flats is B flat, three flats is E flat. And he said, now, when you go down a two-foot time, he said, raise up your foot. I said, I raise up my foot. And he said, now, down your foot. He said, now that's up and down. One, two, one, two, one, two, one, two. He said, now, three-fourth time, that's a waltz. He said, now you make, put your feet down one, and push it this way, two, then raise it up, three. One, two, three. One, two, three. All right, I continue, and I was inheriting that. Then, looked at the book, when I get home, I studied. I got it. Then, he said, four, four times. Well, I said, one, two, three, four. One, two, three, four. I said, man, a lot of takes, and I hear you all play it fast sometimes. Well, he said, well, that's a 6-8. I said, well, how would that go? He said, bum, bum, bum, bum, up and down. I said, well, that's a 6-8. I said, well, all right, man, I'll just practice and inherit all that, and I got it. Now, I don't say nothing about it.
I know. Manuel Mineta teaches all of those same kind of things. Manuel Mineta? He teaches time like that, too, and all that.

I'm talking about Manuel. That is my brother's best friend, him and Freddie. He used to play violin. When Freddie was playing cornet, he used to be, and him and Freddie, every time you see Freddie, you see him. They used to go at this fellow, what they call Henry Morton. Henry Morton's place, they used to go up on Second and Magazine. Well, that was a fine place. Oh, it was a fine place. I don't know if you heard talk about this fellow here, what they call him again, this here fellow, I can't forget it, I can't, John Rucker. No? He was a good comedian. Well, them three used to be together. He was good. We used to play for him at the economy hall, you know. But he was fine. He was a good comedian. But talk about this man here, Manuel, I will, I ain't seen him since the time you brought him here. He came by here a year ago. And I sure was glad to see him. Of course, he didn't, he didn't fain away a little bit though, you know. Well, you see, my daddy was in the same boat as him. See, just like him and my daddy, same color, but of course he done got like a lemon, you know. So that's why I said, well, I said, well, we can't always be the same way all the time. But my daddy is a perfect position. From a piano, and what they call them things that works on them post there, the Calliope, eh?
Oh, yes.

Calliope, he can play that. Because I say, yeah. Well, he played with P. Roy and all of them. See? Now, of course, this fellow, yeah, they tell me, I ain't seen him yet. But I told my cousin Warnick that the old man will fit this Pajou's place will be Peter Bocard. And they tell me he's in the band.
Yeah, he's been playing with the Urican.
They tell me he's in the band.
Albert Warner is your, uh... That's my first cousin.

Your first cousin. Yeah. Well, he ain't been playing as long as me. No. Yeah, he come out with a horn. The bell must have been about that big. Old horn he had. And he started learning. And I believe Shalini learned him. I'd play a trampoline. So that's make, I says, well, I says, now, I said, Warnick, I say, Pajou's dead now, eh? I say, he said, yeah, I don't know who they got. I said, well, the best man would fit that would be, Charlie Love or Peter Bocard. Of course, I said, I don't say that they got a rag. Well, this fella here, he wasn't too much of a rag. He wasn't much of a ragtime man. He wasn't a jazz. Of course, this fella here, what they call like Brimfield and this other fella here, I forgot his name. Never drink, never bummed, never drank, never done nothing. Now I went home. He turned right around and he died. Yeah, that's right.
You can't tell what's going to kill you.

It's no use. When you've got to die, you've got to die. It's no use. And it's no use to cry. See, like some time I got in the wake, I said, well, I said, you know, I looked down at a fellow, they had a fellow died the other day. I didn't know him. They say he used to play bass.
Oh yes, Morris, Joe Morris.
Oh, Joe Morris, well I didn't know him. I went and looked at him unless I seen him so long. He was right down low pace. Oh yes.
I didn't know him, no. Once we, I know Slowdrag bought his bass in 1945. Yeah, well they say he gave up music. He gave up music.

They tell me he used to play with Sam, Sam Morgan and Chris Kelly. Might have been, I don't know who he was. I don't know, but I told all the people. I went and looked at him. You didn't know him? No, my wife said go and see the father. I said, I'll say no.
I never did know him, but I did, once when I made some records.

Mr. Richardson, I see you somewhere, and I hollered at you. But in case they're a stranger, well, I'd be lost. I wouldn't know what they want from me. Well, I was going to ask what happened to your old bass too, Lord. Have you still got that one? That old brass clip?

That was noon, is it. Huh? Was that noon? Yeah, I wanted to ask you some more about guitar, if you have a little bit of time to talk about that. It's right there. If there's anything you can tell us about the different styles, the way they used to play, different kinds of beats. I know you used to do this sort of double time and all on it.
Well, yeah.
Were you the only one that did that, or what kind of thing?

I believe I done showed you, because I done showed, I believe I have, totally right, just like I said, we all have a guess. Let's make, they have rubbers on a passel, you know? Yeah, were you the only one? I believe sometime back I told you about it, that I, that I has taken plaids, and they got some of them, people didn't understand them raps. I got a friend around the corner, they call him Walter.
What was that?
He cat, uh.
Over at Pickus, Black Walter, they call him?

Yeah, he cat. Walter Nelson. He's a good picker, but of course he, Pico asked him, he says, well, he asked me to, Pico asked me to play something, you know, and they was playing, Pico was playing, and I, I take the guitar, he said, now that's my friend. So he said, now Walter, give him your guitar, because I used to play with Lloyd Allen, and he said, give me, he said, yeah. So anyhow, Pico taken the clarinet and started playing. Pico started playing. Then I started making them double raps. But he got through, he says, Walter, can you do that? He said, no, I never did have tried that. He said, you're right, not only you, many others, because Lloyd's the only one I've ever seen making them double raps. He said, now, of course, you picked, but, so then I, he got a son, he was learning. So anyhow, I told him, it's all in the wrist. I told, of course, I try to be friendly with all of them. I said, Walter, I said, it's all in the wrist. That's all. One, two, three, four. I'll tell him, just like you're taking God and playing. No. And I'll tell him like that. Then when I want, if you want me to catch on to that, you want this, Neil? Yeah, let's do it. Now, it's like I said, well, I'm going to play this thing in D natural. I said, yeah, flat. Keep, Keep, Keep, Keep, Keep, Keep, Keep, Keep I have to end the key of A flat. Now I'm going to put this in G natural. I have to end the key of A flat. I am the only one that I have here. I know how I find you. I have to end the key of your dream. I know how I find you. Now that's the way I make them people jelp, you know, Mr. Bill. Now I'm going to say, now listen, I want all you cats to jelp. Hi. I want all you cats to jelps. I want all you cats to jelps. I want all you cats to jelps. That's the way I make them jelps sometimes. Of course, you know how it is when I used to be. My arm, my wrist was stronger than what it is today. You know, you can't put 15 with 72. You know, when you get 72 years old, your wrists, your legs, your mind. Of course, I don't want to say the other thing. All that gets weak on you. See? Yeah. And of course you... Nothing wrong with your mind. You got a good memory.
You got good remembrance. You know, you got to have that. Yeah, you got that. You got to work on your mind.
You got to put two and two together. And you look as young as you ever did. Yeah, yeah, yeah. Well, I tell you. You don't get that. You don't get that.
You don't get that. You don't get that. You don't get that. Yeah, yeah, yeah. You don't change. You know why? Not over 40 to 50, I'd say. You know why?

I'll tell you why I look the same as I do. Of course, a lot of people say the same thing. But I'm not trying to fool God, but I'm fooling the people in the world. That's right. Your hair isn't even gray. That's all right. I can leave it gray, neither. Because if it get too gray, I'm going to take and get me a sun-bodied or something and put on my hair and put a rag or something, borrow my wife's old stuff back there and put on a hair and I'll go to bed and won't let her see it. Well, they got too much stuff going on these days in time to let yourself go down.
Yeah, that's right.

Because the drunk stores sell it for women, why not they can't sell it for the men? Eh? The women folks are just fixing up their eyebrows. They take and do everything. A poor man is always eating, they never advertising that for him. So he just have to study for himself and God am I for all. So you see, the best way to do it, when you take it, you know, the main thing is that when you take and see it, you going down, don't leave yourself going down. If you see where you got any trouble, don't worry about the trouble. If you got anything to do, go on and do it and don't worry about it. If you ain't got nothing, stay without nothing. So if in case you take, try and get your heads all excited and all upset and lose your mind and lose your, I mean, lose and everything else, well then you just naturally up to Eskreek. See, and the whole thing is you just have to take it, take the Lord's name in vain. And then you'll get by these days in town. But if you don't, shame on you. Shame on you. You that's right, Mr. Bill? So you got to just take the world like it come. Because I just natural figure, 72, next month I'll be 73 on February the 2nd. Of course I'm not ashamed to say it because I feel so good. Those things worries me is that cataract on the eye. And the doctors don't look like they want to do nothing with it. Because they don't want to even hurt my skin, they want to even hurt my eyes. So that's why they just leave me to see if I can wear it off. But I'd be glad if in case they cut it off. But the whole thing is they ain't going to do it. Because they look like they like me just that much.
Well I was going to ask, well I think I was having to think, does your wife still sing? I know she used to sing a lot of the spirituals and gospel things.
Oh she was probably nine then, since she'd been contacting with my sister back then. She never was about it, you know.
Is she singing any church?
No, she ain't singing no church. Sometimes she'd get at church, you know, sing different things.
Which church did she go to?
Well she goes to Catholic Church now. Catholic Church now.
Was your family Catholic when you were young? Oh yeah, I was. You were all Catholic.

We all Catholic, yeah. Of course I understand. You know sometimes you get persuaded by something else, you know. And of course I was christened Catholic. Yeah. And I was persuaded by a lot of botched undertaker. Uh huh. Friends of mine, like I said, playing the bands. Well they, they weren't a person like you, they want you to be with them. Yeah, that's right. So you see I was Catholic and of course after I got certain aids, well they persuaded me. They wanted me to join masons. Well, I didn't, I didn't know. So then I found a way, LaBotte. The fellow used to live two blocks from Young. He was man, so he was a man. He used to like me also. He used to call me sandpaper, you know, cause I used to rub that sandpaper together. Oh yeah, that's right.
You told us about that I think the other time we made the tape. Yeah, it's a call sandpaper. Like a drummer does.
And then after that this fellow here, George, but he's dead now I guess. He used to be with Slow Drag. Yeah. He picked it up after me. And with Loon and all too, I think. Yeah, that's Loon.
That bunch.

Yeah, with a little kazoo band. Yeah. So finished down there, they joined, they asked me to join. I said, well, you know what they done? They put a basket for me and they brought me. They made me join the masons. Well, I stayed in there and after they put the basket for me and paid my fears, one black ball can kill you. Yeah. But I didn't know that. But then they joined me and I had no friends, no enemies, all white balls. Turn around, I went to class of crystal. Went and take them out to the first degree. I learned that and stayed in there. Well, after the fellas died and everything else, stayed in there and then I'll see what I lost my job, never had no job. Depression taking place. I had to give up. And I wasn't good. So they wanted to find out how come I don't be there. So I said, well, the reason why I don't be up there is because my financial don't call for it. I ain't got it. Well, the first thing, no, nobody said nothing about it no more. Well, they put me in there and this is the way they put me in there, on nothing. I got out there on nothing. See? Yeah, that's right. So I just got out. So when I done, I said, well, the whole thing is you got to belong to some church or another. It ain't the idea of belonging to a church and it's going to save you, no. But it's just the idea of passing your body through the natural people with saw no head walking around saying he didn't belong to no church. But at any time you could take a poison diet, you could just send them to the graveyard. You know? Yeah. Once you're just going and putting flowers. You can't smell no flowers. Huh? No. It's the same thing as I was asking the fellow there. I said, sir, I was sorry asking that because he put a tab on me. He says, Kepney says, I now says, John, John P. John P. They call him John P. Lewis. I said, listen. I said, how come when y'all, the Chinese men die, they put red beans and rice? I said, what make they put that? He said, what? I said, well, I know that. It doesn't make a catastrophe in that. He said, what make they put, what? I said, what make they put red bean rice at the tomb? He said, what make they put flowers at the grave at the other people? I said, well, I didn't know what make myself. And I know they put flowers, but I didn't know I was lost. And he had me. Now he's waiting for an answer from me, and I was waiting for an answer from him. Well, he's one of them. But he gave me an answer. He said, no, you people put flowers at the grave. No smell. You can't smell. I said, well, Dan, what you got to do about the red beans and rice? He said, we put it out because y'all put it in the flowers. But he said, well, he could eat them when he wake up. Yeah. You know, smell of flowers? That's for the people what's on the outside. Yeah. See? And the red beans and rice is for the people what's living. And the flowers is for the people what? Is in there smelling flowers. Now, what's that you want to say, Mr. Russell?

Well, I was asking about your wife singing. I guess that's how we got into that. Oh, yeah. First, I was wondering if there's anything else about the guitar. You can tell in the old days, did they just hit the four beats usually? Or how did they do? The oldest guitar players you've ever heard? Well, I'll tell you.
Some of them, of course I...
Like some of the old fellas with Manuel Perez's early bands and those kind of bands that you've heard.

Well, I'll tell you. Some of them, you see, like I was telling a fella the other day, I say, you know, he said, what's the name of that guitar? I said, well, this is a, that's that stupid. So that's the way, he said, what kind of, he said, well, what you playing? I said, this is what they call a electric guitar. And he had one. I said, now listen, this is a electric guitar you gonna play with me? And I said, now make A natural. So, I, that, that, that, like that. And he plays, they make an A natural. He was hitting the little E. I said, now you ain't right. So he said, he said, yeah, you ain't right. I said, I'm making A. You turn up your A with mine. So he said, no, this is. I said, it's bound to go higher. So I looked at him, I said, now listen, do you see what's the matter? I'll tell you what's the matter. You, I'm not gonna cold water you, but you is a better musician than me. I know that, because I will say that all the time. He said, no, I say, you see, you know, I said, they ain't nothing but the reading music, but I qualified you as the better musician than me. I said, you see, you see what I'm playing, when I'm playing this, you making something else? He said, yeah. I said, well, the reason why, because you see, this is the electric guitar, and you got a gas guitar. So you see, I'm playing by the liquor, and he's playing by the gas. I don't care.
I wonder, in the old days, just with the band, when they'd play with the band, just, did they use just mostly cards, or did they put in other little runs, or? Cards. What style did they play?

Well, they, they, they, they're playing straight. Like that. Oh, I want a bad lead. See the bad lead? Same with the voice of singing. Yeah. See, that's the way they just give that right straight beat. That's straight beat. And that's better. You know, it's better. But of course, when some of them want to take and make them double raps, they get messed up, messed up for that other fella. Yeah. See? Of course, everybody's saying. It's like, I would be making them double raps, but I would be holding the same at the right time. But somebody else will mess up that other fella, trying to follow him. Yeah. And he's, he's, he's, he's, he's talking about that other fella playing. Yeah. See, it's just the same thing as you're talking. It's just the same thing as you're talking with. It's just the same thing as you're talking with. It's just the same thing as you're talking with. It's just the same thing as you're talking with. It's just the same thing as you're talking with. It's just as you're talking with. . . . See, well that's straight time, that's a good time. Let the other fella do the variation. That's what the piano is the same way. If you're playing on that piano, you've got your right hand for the triple clap. You see? And your left hand, bass right behind. Boom, boom. And that's your . He can make all this variation on the right hand with the triple clap. Ain't that right? So it is in . One, two, three, four. One, two, three, four. One, two, three, four. One, two, three. One, two, three. One, two, three. One, two, three, four. One, two, three. gosh . . . You can talk to me. You know something? I'm going to take the photo to Al Street. I'm going to buy a whole stuante. And I'm going to tell you one thing when I come out. I'm going to paint the whole towel red. I don't care who like it, who's dead, who's living. You know something, Mr. Bill? I just got to be no fool man. I'll be talking and talking and talking. Now, you can believe it or not. Someday, I'm going to take a telephone where they get off of. But I don't care if they're right or wrong. But I'm going to tell them when they come here. See, Mr. Bill is right there for you. If you know his name, I'll tell it to you. Go see him with your troubles. What is the name of that tune, Lewis? What's that? What's the name of that tune you were playing? Is there any name to it? Ask me and I'll ask you. I don't know. I just made it up. You made it up. I don't know. I just started that whole thing. That's make up to you. My mind going calm. I didn't know what I was doing. But I just started that whole thing. Well, it sounds good, eh? Yeah, it sounds nice.
Well, you see? Well, I just started that whole thing. Like you say, you can just talk anything to it, too.

It sounds like it's coming to you talking or anything. Foolishness. It's the same thing as this father Louis Armstrong. Half the time, he didn't know what he was saying. But he just, don't you take notice? Yeah, that's right. But everybody gets a kick out of it. That's the tool and everybody enjoys it. Yeah. Well, I ain't following behind him. It's just nothing in me. I like foolishness anyhow. I'll see the right carousel. I like it. And I'm going to die with it. I guess if I was a young man it'd be different. But I've got this age and I've still got foolishness in me. You know I can't stop. Well.

Well, I was going to ask you about, unless you have something else in mind, about the kind of a beat you'd play for a waltz on the guitar. Say with a band. One, two, three. Yeah. Would you just play on the second and third beat or on all three beats? Or how do you do it? With a band. One, two, three. One, one.

See, I down beat the bass. Yeah, that's for the bass, huh? It's gosh. It's not as usual as usual. It's not as usual as usual. I'm going to go to the Holy Hill and I know that different here and I'm glad to receive them. Anytime they come here they will come. Two men that be here all the time. And I know that I'm glad to receive them. And they like that pretty wall. I know they enjoy them. It's only gosh. It's only gosh. It's only gosh. It's only gosh. It's only gosh. . Thank you. You know, you know, you've been keeping that check hard, hard, hard all the time for me. You know, you know you're so secure and you know you get an old penny. You know, every time I turn around, you're always messing with me. You know, you always cut my check and I know that well. I always do believe in you, take and do the right thing. I know that well, you're the right thing. Now look at that guy. Who do you think the governor is thinking about? The governor is always looking for Louis Capel. Well, I know what Louis Capel, who's here? He ain't nobody. Who do you think you is? Eh? What, what, what do you think you... Well, woman, you know, well, I've been working at the Visual Flush all my days. And that's why I take you a little bullet, bullet from. Now, wait, I'm gonna tell you, I'm gonna leave you now. And I know I'm gonna, I can just tell you goodbye. Oh, goodbye. I used to imitate a woman good, but I couldn't, I couldn't so well, you know.
It's hard on your voice, I guess, to try to talk up too high, isn't it?

Yeah, I used to take it, sometime I'd get around, I used to see a woman come to see her, and I'd get out there and I'd see them coming in the front door or something, and they'd go in around. I'd say, good morning, Mr. Willey. Good morning. Oh, that's the old one. And then I'd put my hands over my mother. Listen, Willey, do you find it across, eh? Yes, ma'am. I said, well, all right, bring me a pong of red beans. Oh, that's the... Maybe you're right, huh? Yeah. You want to go back there and talk with her, you know? Uh-huh. Now, what else can I put on? You'll stand about something now.

I was gonna ask you for one thing, if we have room here, if not we'll do it on another reel, if you have a few minutes yet. If you could tell us anything about the dancing in the old... Well, the dancing... ...the old times. I mean, what kind of steps did they use, or is it much different than now?

It's a big difference from now to today. Them different dances, what they had today... I'm gonna put it on this here, a guitar, wow. Sure, sure, put it on. And, uh, you see the dances, them did, uh... Everybody was dipping... ...of where dancing... ...but they never had nobody throwing one another over one another's backs. They used to take in dance... ...and every one of them coming there, they had to be women... ...or they had to be men. ...but they couldn't get in, in the dances. Women, it's women. Now they're giving a concert for children. That's a concert for children. But, of course, these days in town, when they give a concert for children, the women is in the contract. The old women is in the contract. Old-grade women, everything goes. But when they said, children, them days in town, it was children. Well, excuse me for interrupting.

I remember that over here at Economy Hall... Economy Hall... ...and they'd give these concerts on Sunday night or so, I remember... ...toke... ...well, people like Lizzie Miles would sing... Well, Liz would sing... ...and Wilhelmina Barth used to play... ...and Bunk says he used to play... ...were those sort of like dances, or were they really a concert? It is a concert. It's a concert. You know, some cities will have a law against giving a dance on a Sunday night, so they'll call them concerts, but it'll be the same as another dance any other night. Well, no... Is this the same as another dance, or a different...

It was only a majority of the time at the Economy Hall, it was on a Sunday night. Was it a real concert band or not? Sometime we gave a concert on a Sunday night. Mr. Toko, he used to run in concert because he used to have them cheering... ...and old folks to act. They used to have a stage in front, downstairs in the back, and they'd put a... ...a false stage up. Yeah. With what they call them, horses? Yeah, on those trestles and then a platform up on there. Well, they'd put a...make a stand, stand on there. Well, the people would get on top there and dance, and they'd make a little partation, so they can go back in the back, so they can make the...to the dressing room. Then they'd come out on another side of the curtain, then they'd come out on the stage. Yeah. But you see, now, these here, what you asked me about, these here people... It's on a Sunday. Well, you see... ...a half.
You were talking about the concerts over at the Economy Hall.

Yes, that concert, what we used to give. Well, they had that old Peter Pocan. He used to play for some of them. He's from over the river. And he used to be the director. He used to be the leader. He was a better leader than Piron. You know, because Piron wasn't the leader.
